case_info.scenario: A healthy 25-year-old woman was seen in the cardiology clinic 1 month after being diagnosed with an upper respiratory tract infection during an emergency department visit for 2 days of shortness of breath and low-grade fevers. A computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiogram performed in the emergency department revealed no pulmonary infiltrates, effusion, or embolism but identified an isolated 4.2-cm dilatation in the mid ascending aorta (Figure 1). In the cardiology clinic, her blood pressure was 118/85 mm/Hg and heart rate 65/min. A transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) demonstrated normal left and right ventricular function, a 4.3-cm ascending aortic aneurysm, and a bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) without evidence of aortic stenosis or regurgitation (Figure 1). Family history revealed that her father had a dissection of the ascending aorta repaired at age 60 years.

case_info.caption: A, Non–electrocardiogram-gated computed tomography scan of the chest obtained in the emergency department. Transthoracic echocardiography performed in the cardiology clinic demonstrated an ascending aortic aneurysm (B) and a bicuspid aortic valve (C).
case_info.explanation: Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm (ATAA) and BAV B. Order an aortic electrocardiogram (ECG)-gated CT angiogram with contrast. The key to correct management is recognizing that an ascending aortic aneurysm detected on a standard imaging study should be evaluated with specialized CT imaging timed to diastole (ECG-gated;Figure 2) to reduce cardiac motion artifact. Choice A is incorrect because the patient did not meet indications for urgent surgical repair. Surveillance decisions (choice C) are appropriate only after fully evaluating the aneurysm. β-Blocker treatment (choice D) is not indicated with normal blood pressure. Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms involve dilation of the aortic root and/or ascending aorta extending into the proximal aortic arch and affect approximately 5.3 per 100 000 individuals per year worldwide.1Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm may expand asymptomatically and cause aortic rupture, which is associated with a mortality rate greater than 90%.1Incidence of ATAA is increased among individuals with BAV, which has a worldwide prevalence of 1% to 2%,2and among those with a family history of aortic dissection, familial connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome), or Turner syndrome.3Rarely, ATAAs are caused by syphilis or rheumatologic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or Takayasu disease.3Up to 56% of patients with BAV younger than age 30 years have a dilated ascending aorta (diameter 1.1 times greater than expected based on age, sex, and body surface area).2Patients with BAV have an approximately 9-fold increased relative risk for aortic dissection, although their absolute risk is low (0.68% lifetime).2,3A 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline recommended that first-degree relatives of patients with BAV, aortic root or ascending aorta aneurysms, or aortic dissection undergo aortic screening with a TTE, ECG-gated CT angiography, or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the thoracic aorta and that patients with familial BAV and/or thoracic aortic aneurysms should be referred for genetic testing.3 Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms are frequently diagnosed incidentally on a thoracic CT imaging study. Approximately 95% of patients with ATAA are asymptomatic at diagnosis, and 5% have nonspecific symptoms such as chest pain, back pain, dysphagia, or dyspnea.4Patients with ATAA should be evaluated for connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and family history of BAV, aortic aneurysm, and sudden death should be elicited. A TTE to evaluate left ventricular function, aortic valve, root, and the proximal ascending aorta, and an ECG-gated aortic CT angiogram with contrast, should be obtained. Thoracic aorta MRA is an alternative to CT and has similar sensitivity (100% vs 98%, respectively) and specificity (98% vs 98%, respectively) for aneurysm detection.5 For patients with ATAA, the 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline–recommended goal systolic blood pressure is less than 130/80 mm Hg.6The guideline recommends that patients with BAV who have an ascending aortic diameter 5.5 cm or greater undergo surgery to replace the aortic root and ascending aorta. Other surgical indications include ascending aortic cross-sectional area-height ratio 10 cm2/m or greater or aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater with risk factors for aortic dissection such as family history of aortic dissection, rapid aortic growth rate (>0.3 cm/y), or preconception in women with BAV and an aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater.6,7Patients with ATAA and BAV who do not meet indications for surgery should undergo annual echocardiography, CT, or MRA to assess for rapid aneurysm expansion (>0.3 cm/y) and progression of BAV.6 Surgical repair includes replacement of aneurysmal tissue with a polyester fiber conduit. For patients with ATAA and severe bicuspid aortic valve stenosis (aortic velocity >4 m/s, mean pressure gradient >40 mm Hg, aortic valve area <1.0 cm2) or aortic regurgitation, aortic valve replacement is typically recommended.6Surgery can often be performed through minimally invasive procedures, such as a hemisternotomy.8The 5-year survival rate after ascending aortic and root replacement is 89.9%.9After ATAA surgery, patients should receive surveillance imaging with CT or MRA within 1 year and, if stable, every 5 years thereafter to monitor for progression of aortic dilation.6 A ECG-gated CT angiogram demonstrated a 5.0-cm ATAA with a cross-sectional/height ratio of 11.7 cm2/m (Figure 2). Based on the patient’s aortic aneurysm size and family history of aortic dissection, she met criteria for surgery.3Ascending aortic replacement was performed minimally invasively, with 4 cm of ascending aorta excised and replaced with a polyester fiber conduit. She did not undergo aortic valve repair or replacement due to her young age and absence of aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation. She was discharged after a 4-day hospitalization. At a clinic visit 1 month later, the patient was asymptomatic and blood pressure was 110/80 mm Hg. Aortic surveillance will be performed with a ECG-gated CT scan 12 months postoperatively, and her first-degree relatives were offered screening for BAV and aortic aneurysm.

Given the patient's young age and the size of the ascending aortic aneurysm at 4.3 cm, immediate surgical intervention is not yet indicated. [NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm (ATAA) and BAV B. Order an aortic electrocardiogram (ECG)-gated CT angiogram with contrast. The key to correct management is recognizing that an ascending aortic aneurysm detected on a standard imaging study should be evaluated with specialized CT imaging timed to diastole (ECG-gated;Figure 2) to reduce cardiac motion artifact. Choice A is incorrect because the patient did not meet indications for urgent surgical repair. Surveillance decisions (choice C) are appropriate only after fully evaluating the aneurysm. β-Blocker treatment (choice D) is not indicated with normal blood pressure. Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms involve dilation of the aortic root and/or ascending aorta extending into the proximal aortic arch and affect approximately 5.3 per 100 000 individuals per year worldwide.1Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm may expand asymptomatically and cause aortic rupture, which is associated with a mortality rate greater than 90%.1Incidence of ATAA is increased among individuals with BAV, which has a worldwide prevalence of 1% to 2%,2and among those with a family history of aortic dissection, familial connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome), or Turner syndrome.3Rarely, ATAAs are caused by syphilis or rheumatologic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or Takayasu disease.3Up to 56% of patients with BAV younger than age 30 years have a dilated ascending aorta (diameter 1.1 times greater than expected based on age, sex, and body surface area).2Patients with BAV have an approximately 9-fold increased relative risk for aortic dissection, although their absolute risk is low (0.68% lifetime).2,3A 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline recommended that first-degree relatives of patients with BAV, aortic root or ascending aorta aneurysms, or aortic dissection undergo aortic screening with a TTE, ECG-gated CT angiography, or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the thoracic aorta and that patients with familial BAV and/or thoracic aortic aneurysms should be referred for genetic testing.3 Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms are frequently diagnosed incidentally on a thoracic CT imaging study. Approximately 95% of patients with ATAA are asymptomatic at diagnosis, and 5% have nonspecific symptoms such as chest pain, back pain, dysphagia, or dyspnea.4Patients with ATAA should be evaluated for connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and family history of BAV, aortic aneurysm, and sudden death should be elicited. A TTE to evaluate left ventricular function, aortic valve, root, and the proximal ascending aorta, and an ECG-gated aortic CT angiogram with contrast, should be obtained. Thoracic aorta MRA is an alternative to CT and has similar sensitivity (100% vs 98%, respectively) and specificity (98% vs 98%, respectively) for aneurysm detection.5 For patients with ATAA, the 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline–recommended goal systolic blood pressure is less than 130/80 mm Hg.6The guideline recommends that patients with BAV who have an ascending aortic diameter 5.5 cm or greater undergo surgery to replace the aortic root and ascending aorta. Other surgical indications include ascending aortic cross-sectional area-height ratio 10 cm2/m or greater or aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater with risk factors for aortic dissection such as family history of aortic dissection, rapid aortic growth rate (>0.3 cm/y), or preconception in women with BAV and an aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater.6,7Patients with ATAA and BAV who do not meet indications for surgery should undergo annual echocardiography, CT, or MRA to assess for rapid aneurysm expansion (>0.3 cm/y) and progression of BAV.6 Surgical repair includes replacement of aneurysmal tissue with a polyester fiber conduit. For patients with ATAA and severe bicuspid aortic valve stenosis (aortic velocity >4 m/s, mean pressure gradient >40 mm Hg, aortic valve area <1.0 cm2) or aortic regurgitation, aortic valve replacement is typically recommended.6Surgery can often be performed through minimally invasive procedures, such as a hemisternotomy.8The 5-year survival rate after ascending aortic and root replacement is 89.9%.9After ATAA surgery, patients should receive surveillance imaging with CT or MRA within 1 year and, if stable, every 5 years thereafter to monitor for progression of aortic dilation.6 A ECG-gated CT angiogram demonstrated a 5.0-cm ATAA with a cross-sectional/height ratio of 11.7 cm2/m (Figure 2). Based on the patient’s aortic aneurysm size and family history of aortic dissection, she met criteria for surgery.3Ascending aortic replacement was performed minimally invasively, with 4 cm of ascending aorta excised and replaced with a polyester fiber conduit. She did not undergo aortic valve repair or replacement due to her young age and absence of aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation. She was discharged after a 4-day hospitalization. At a clinic visit 1 month later, the patient was asymptomatic and blood pressure was 110/80 mm Hg. Aortic surveillance will be performed with a ECG-gated CT scan 12 months postoperatively, and her first-degree relatives were offered screening for BAV and aortic aneurysm.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A healthy 25-year-old woman was seen in the cardiology clinic 1 month after being diagnosed with an upper respiratory tract infection during an emergency department visit for 2 days of shortness of breath and low-grade fevers. A computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiogram performed in the emergency department revealed no pulmonary infiltrates, effusion, or embolism but identified an isolated 4.2-cm dilatation in the mid ascending aorta (Figure 1). A transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) demonstrated normal left and right ventricular function, a 4.3-cm ascending aortic aneurysm, and a bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) without evidence of aortic stenosis or regurgitation (Figure 1). Family history revealed that her father had a dissection of the ascending aorta repaired at age 60 years.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered

  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your

}

workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]

[Confidence]

  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 2.2. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)

  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm (ATAA) and BAV B. Order an aortic electrocardiogram (ECG)-gated CT angiogram with contrast. The key to correct management is recognizing that an ascending aortic aneurysm detected on a standard imaging study should be evaluated with specialized CT imaging timed to diastole (ECG-gated;Figure 2) to reduce cardiac motion artifact. Choice A is incorrect because the patient did not meet indications for urgent surgical repair. Surveillance decisions (choice C) are appropriate only after fully evaluating the aneurysm. β-Blocker treatment (choice D) is not indicated with normal blood pressure. Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms involve dilation of the aortic root and/or ascending aorta extending into the proximal aortic arch and affect approximately 5.3 per 100 000 individuals per year worldwide.1Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm may expand asymptomatically and cause aortic rupture, which is associated with a mortality rate greater than 90%.1Incidence of ATAA is increased among individuals with BAV, which has a worldwide prevalence of 1% to 2%,2and among those with a family history of aortic dissection, familial connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome), or Turner syndrome.3Rarely, ATAAs are caused by syphilis or rheumatologic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or Takayasu disease.3Up to 56% of patients with BAV younger than age 30 years have a dilated ascending aorta (diameter 1.1 times greater than expected based on age, sex, and body surface area).2Patients with BAV have an approximately 9-fold increased relative risk for aortic dissection, although their absolute risk is low (0.68% lifetime).2,3A 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline recommended that first-degree relatives of patients with BAV, aortic root or ascending aorta aneurysms, or aortic dissection undergo aortic screening with a TTE, ECG-gated CT angiography, or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the thoracic aorta and that patients with familial BAV and/or thoracic aortic aneurysms should be referred for genetic testing.3 Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms are frequently diagnosed incidentally on a thoracic CT imaging study. Approximately 95% of patients with ATAA are asymptomatic at diagnosis, and 5% have nonspecific symptoms such as chest pain, back pain, dysphagia, or dyspnea.4Patients with ATAA should be evaluated for connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and family history of BAV, aortic aneurysm, and sudden death should be elicited. A TTE to evaluate left ventricular function, aortic valve, root, and the proximal ascending aorta, and an ECG-gated aortic CT angiogram with contrast, should be obtained. Thoracic aorta MRA is an alternative to CT and has similar sensitivity (100% vs 98%, respectively) and specificity (98% vs 98%, respectively) for aneurysm detection.5 For patients with ATAA, the 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline–recommended goal systolic blood pressure is less than 130/80 mm Hg.6The guideline recommends that patients with BAV who have an ascending aortic diameter 5.5 cm or greater undergo surgery to replace the aortic root and ascending aorta. Other surgical indications include ascending aortic cross-sectional area-height ratio 10 cm2/m or greater or aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater with risk factors for aortic dissection such as family history of aortic dissection, rapid aortic growth rate (>0.3 cm/y), or preconception in women with BAV and an aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater.6,7Patients with ATAA and BAV who do not meet indications for surgery should undergo annual echocardiography, CT, or MRA to assess for rapid aneurysm expansion (>0.3 cm/y) and progression of BAV.6 Surgical repair includes replacement of aneurysmal tissue with a polyester fiber conduit. For patients with ATAA and severe bicuspid aortic valve stenosis (aortic velocity >4 m/s, mean pressure gradient >40 mm Hg, aortic valve area <1.0 cm2) or aortic regurgitation, aortic valve replacement is typically recommended.6Surgery can often be performed through minimally invasive procedures, such as a hemisternotomy.8The 5-year survival rate after ascending aortic and root replacement is 89.9%.9After ATAA surgery, patients should receive surveillance imaging with CT or MRA within 1 year and, if stable, every 5 years thereafter to monitor for progression of aortic dilation.6 A ECG-gated CT angiogram demonstrated a 5.0-cm ATAA with a cross-sectional/height ratio of 11.7 cm2/m (Figure 2). Based on the patient’s aortic aneurysm size and family history of aortic dissection, she met criteria for surgery.3Ascending aortic replacement was performed minimally invasively, with 4 cm of ascending aorta excised and replaced with a polyester fiber conduit. She did not undergo aortic valve repair or replacement due to her young age and absence of aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation. She was discharged after a 4-day hospitalization. At a clinic visit 1 month later, the patient was asymptomatic and blood pressure was 110/80 mm Hg. Aortic surveillance will be performed with a ECG-gated CT scan 12 months postoperatively, and her first-degree relatives were offered screening for BAV and aortic aneurysm.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.

case_info.caption: A, Non–electrocardiogram-gated computed tomography scan of the chest obtained in the emergency department. Transthoracic echocardiography performed in the cardiology clinic demonstrated an ascending aortic aneurysm (B) and a bicuspid aortic valve (C).
case_info.explanation: Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm (ATAA) and BAV B. Order an aortic electrocardiogram (ECG)-gated CT angiogram with contrast. The key to correct management is recognizing that an ascending aortic aneurysm detected on a standard imaging study should be evaluated with specialized CT imaging timed to diastole (ECG-gated;Figure 2) to reduce cardiac motion artifact. Choice A is incorrect because the patient did not meet indications for urgent surgical repair. Surveillance decisions (choice C) are appropriate only after fully evaluating the aneurysm. β-Blocker treatment (choice D) is not indicated with normal blood pressure. Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms involve dilation of the aortic root and/or ascending aorta extending into the proximal aortic arch and affect approximately 5.3 per 100 000 individuals per year worldwide.1Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm may expand asymptomatically and cause aortic rupture, which is associated with a mortality rate greater than 90%.1Incidence of ATAA is increased among individuals with BAV, which has a worldwide prevalence of 1% to 2%,2and among those with a family history of aortic dissection, familial connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome), or Turner syndrome.3Rarely, ATAAs are caused by syphilis or rheumatologic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or Takayasu disease.3Up to 56% of patients with BAV younger than age 30 years have a dilated ascending aorta (diameter 1.1 times greater than expected based on age, sex, and body surface area).2Patients with BAV have an approximately 9-fold increased relative risk for aortic dissection, although their absolute risk is low (0.68% lifetime).2,3A 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline recommended that first-degree relatives of patients with BAV, aortic root or ascending aorta aneurysms, or aortic dissection undergo aortic screening with a TTE, ECG-gated CT angiography, or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the thoracic aorta and that patients with familial BAV and/or thoracic aortic aneurysms should be referred for genetic testing.3 Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms are frequently diagnosed incidentally on a thoracic CT imaging study. Approximately 95% of patients with ATAA are asymptomatic at diagnosis, and 5% have nonspecific symptoms such as chest pain, back pain, dysphagia, or dyspnea.4Patients with ATAA should be evaluated for connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and family history of BAV, aortic aneurysm, and sudden death should be elicited. A TTE to evaluate left ventricular function, aortic valve, root, and the proximal ascending aorta, and an ECG-gated aortic CT angiogram with contrast, should be obtained. Thoracic aorta MRA is an alternative to CT and has similar sensitivity (100% vs 98%, respectively) and specificity (98% vs 98%, respectively) for aneurysm detection.5 For patients with ATAA, the 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline–recommended goal systolic blood pressure is less than 130/80 mm Hg.6The guideline recommends that patients with BAV who have an ascending aortic diameter 5.5 cm or greater undergo surgery to replace the aortic root and ascending aorta. Other surgical indications include ascending aortic cross-sectional area-height ratio 10 cm2/m or greater or aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater with risk factors for aortic dissection such as family history of aortic dissection, rapid aortic growth rate (>0.3 cm/y), or preconception in women with BAV and an aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater.6,7Patients with ATAA and BAV who do not meet indications for surgery should undergo annual echocardiography, CT, or MRA to assess for rapid aneurysm expansion (>0.3 cm/y) and progression of BAV.6 Surgical repair includes replacement of aneurysmal tissue with a polyester fiber conduit. For patients with ATAA and severe bicuspid aortic valve stenosis (aortic velocity >4 m/s, mean pressure gradient >40 mm Hg, aortic valve area <1.0 cm2) or aortic regurgitation, aortic valve replacement is typically recommended.6Surgery can often be performed through minimally invasive procedures, such as a hemisternotomy.8The 5-year survival rate after ascending aortic and root replacement is 89.9%.9After ATAA surgery, patients should receive surveillance imaging with CT or MRA within 1 year and, if stable, every 5 years thereafter to monitor for progression of aortic dilation.6 A ECG-gated CT angiogram demonstrated a 5.0-cm ATAA with a cross-sectional/height ratio of 11.7 cm2/m (Figure 2). Based on the patient’s aortic aneurysm size and family history of aortic dissection, she met criteria for surgery.3Ascending aortic replacement was performed minimally invasively, with 4 cm of ascending aorta excised and replaced with a polyester fiber conduit. She did not undergo aortic valve repair or replacement due to her young age and absence of aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation. She was discharged after a 4-day hospitalization. At a clinic visit 1 month later, the patient was asymptomatic and blood pressure was 110/80 mm Hg. Aortic surveillance will be performed with a ECG-gated CT scan 12 months postoperatively, and her first-degree relatives were offered screening for BAV and aortic aneurysm.

case_info.explanation: Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm (ATAA) and BAV B. Order an aortic electrocardiogram (ECG)-gated CT angiogram with contrast. The key to correct management is recognizing that an ascending aortic aneurysm detected on a standard imaging study should be evaluated with specialized CT imaging timed to diastole (ECG-gated;Figure 2) to reduce cardiac motion artifact. Choice A is incorrect because the patient did not meet indications for urgent surgical repair. Surveillance decisions (choice C) are appropriate only after fully evaluating the aneurysm. β-Blocker treatment (choice D) is not indicated with normal blood pressure. Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms involve dilation of the aortic root and/or ascending aorta extending into the proximal aortic arch and affect approximately 5.3 per 100 000 individuals per year worldwide.1Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm may expand asymptomatically and cause aortic rupture, which is associated with a mortality rate greater than 90%.1Incidence of ATAA is increased among individuals with BAV, which has a worldwide prevalence of 1% to 2%,2and among those with a family history of aortic dissection, familial connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome), or Turner syndrome.3Rarely, ATAAs are caused by syphilis or rheumatologic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or Takayasu disease.3Up to 56% of patients with BAV younger than age 30 years have a dilated ascending aorta (diameter 1.1 times greater than expected based on age, sex, and body surface area).2Patients with BAV have an approximately 9-fold increased relative risk for aortic dissection, although their absolute risk is low (0.68% lifetime).2,3A 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline recommended that first-degree relatives of patients with BAV, aortic root or ascending aorta aneurysms, or aortic dissection undergo aortic screening with a TTE, ECG-gated CT angiography, or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the thoracic aorta and that patients with familial BAV and/or thoracic aortic aneurysms should be referred for genetic testing.3 Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms are frequently diagnosed incidentally on a thoracic CT imaging study. Approximately 95% of patients with ATAA are asymptomatic at diagnosis, and 5% have nonspecific symptoms such as chest pain, back pain, dysphagia, or dyspnea.4Patients with ATAA should be evaluated for connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and family history of BAV, aortic aneurysm, and sudden death should be elicited. A TTE to evaluate left ventricular function, aortic valve, root, and the proximal ascending aorta, and an ECG-gated aortic CT angiogram with contrast, should be obtained. Thoracic aorta MRA is an alternative to CT and has similar sensitivity (100% vs 98%, respectively) and specificity (98% vs 98%, respectively) for aneurysm detection.5 For patients with ATAA, the 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline–recommended goal systolic blood pressure is less than 130/80 mm Hg.6The guideline recommends that patients with BAV who have an ascending aortic diameter 5.5 cm or greater undergo surgery to replace the aortic root and ascending aorta. Other surgical indications include ascending aortic cross-sectional area-height ratio 10 cm2/m or greater or aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater with risk factors for aortic dissection such as family history of aortic dissection, rapid aortic growth rate (>0.3 cm/y), or preconception in women with BAV and an aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater.6,7Patients with ATAA and BAV who do not meet indications for surgery should undergo annual echocardiography, CT, or MRA to assess for rapid aneurysm expansion (>0.3 cm/y) and progression of BAV.6 Surgical repair includes replacement of aneurysmal tissue with a polyester fiber conduit. [NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.

   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.

   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

4. Frustration

case_info.explanation: Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm (ATAA) and BAV B. Order an aortic electrocardiogram (ECG)-gated CT angiogram with contrast. The key to correct management is recognizing that an ascending aortic aneurysm detected on a standard imaging study should be evaluated with specialized CT imaging timed to diastole (ECG-gated;Figure 2) to reduce cardiac motion artifact. Choice A is incorrect because the patient did not meet indications for urgent surgical repair. Surveillance decisions (choice C) are appropriate only after fully evaluating the aneurysm. β-Blocker treatment (choice D) is not indicated with normal blood pressure. Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms involve dilation of the aortic root and/or ascending aorta extending into the proximal aortic arch and affect approximately 5.3 per 100 000 individuals per year worldwide.1Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm may expand asymptomatically and cause aortic rupture, which is associated with a mortality rate greater than 90%.1Incidence of ATAA is increased among individuals with BAV, which has a worldwide prevalence of 1% to 2%,2and among those with a family history of aortic dissection, familial connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome), or Turner syndrome.3Rarely, ATAAs are caused by syphilis or rheumatologic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or Takayasu disease.3Up to 56% of patients with BAV younger than age 30 years have a dilated ascending aorta (diameter 1.1 times greater than expected based on age, sex, and body surface area).2Patients with BAV have an approximately 9-fold increased relative risk for aortic dissection, although their absolute risk is low (0.68% lifetime).2,3A 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline recommended that first-degree relatives of patients with BAV, aortic root or ascending aorta aneurysms, or aortic dissection undergo aortic screening with a TTE, ECG-gated CT angiography, or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the thoracic aorta and that patients with familial BAV and/or thoracic aortic aneurysms should be referred for genetic testing.3 Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms are frequently diagnosed incidentally on a thoracic CT imaging study. Approximately 95% of patients with ATAA are asymptomatic at diagnosis, and 5% have nonspecific symptoms such as chest pain, back pain, dysphagia, or dyspnea.4Patients with ATAA should be evaluated for connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and family history of BAV, aortic aneurysm, and sudden death should be elicited. A TTE to evaluate left ventricular function, aortic valve, root, and the proximal ascending aorta, and an ECG-gated aortic CT angiogram with contrast, should be obtained. Thoracic aorta MRA is an alternative to CT and has similar sensitivity (100% vs 98%, respectively) and specificity (98% vs 98%, respectively) for aneurysm detection.5 For patients with ATAA, the 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline–recommended goal systolic blood pressure is less than 130/80 mm Hg.6The guideline recommends that patients with BAV who have an ascending aortic diameter 5.5 cm or greater undergo surgery to replace the aortic root and ascending aorta. Other surgical indications include ascending aortic cross-sectional area-height ratio 10 cm2/m or greater or aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater with risk factors for aortic dissection such as family history of aortic dissection, rapid aortic growth rate (>0.3 cm/y), or preconception in women with BAV and an aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater.6,7Patients with ATAA and BAV who do not meet indications for surgery should undergo annual echocardiography, CT, or MRA to assess for rapid aneurysm expansion (>0.3 cm/y) and progression of BAV.6 Surgical repair includes replacement of aneurysmal tissue with a polyester fiber conduit. For patients with ATAA and severe bicuspid aortic valve stenosis (aortic velocity >4 m/s, mean pressure gradient >40 mm Hg, aortic valve area <1.0 cm2) or aortic regurgitation, aortic valve replacement is typically recommended.6Surgery can often be performed through minimally invasive procedures, such as a hemisternotomy.8The 5-year survival rate after ascending aortic and root replacement is 89.9%.9After ATAA surgery, patients should receive surveillance imaging with CT or MRA within 1 year and, if stable, every 5 years thereafter to monitor for progression of aortic dilation.6 A ECG-gated CT angiogram demonstrated a 5.0-cm ATAA with a cross-sectional/height ratio of 11.7 cm2/m (Figure 2). Based on the patient’s aortic aneurysm size and family history of aortic dissection, she met criteria for surgery.3Ascending aortic replacement was performed minimally invasively, with 4 cm of ascending aorta excised and replaced with a polyester fiber conduit. She did not undergo aortic valve repair or replacement due to her young age and absence of aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation. She was discharged after a 4-day hospitalization. At a clinic visit 1 month later, the patient was asymptomatic and blood pressure was 110/80 mm Hg. Aortic surveillance will be performed with a ECG-gated CT scan 12 months postoperatively, and her first-degree relatives were offered screening for BAV and aortic aneurysm.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

   Definition:

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"

       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more

   Definition:

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

case_info.caption: A, Non–electrocardiogram-gated computed tomography scan of the chest obtained in the emergency department. Transthoracic echocardiography performed in the cardiology clinic demonstrated an ascending aortic aneurysm (B) and a bicuspid aortic valve (C).
case_info.explanation: Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm (ATAA) and BAV B. Order an aortic electrocardiogram (ECG)-gated CT angiogram with contrast. The key to correct management is recognizing that an ascending aortic aneurysm detected on a standard imaging study should be evaluated with specialized CT imaging timed to diastole (ECG-gated;Figure 2) to reduce cardiac motion artifact. Choice A is incorrect because the patient did not meet indications for urgent surgical repair. Surveillance decisions (choice C) are appropriate only after fully evaluating the aneurysm. β-Blocker treatment (choice D) is not indicated with normal blood pressure. Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms involve dilation of the aortic root and/or ascending aorta extending into the proximal aortic arch and affect approximately 5.3 per 100 000 individuals per year worldwide.1Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysm may expand asymptomatically and cause aortic rupture, which is associated with a mortality rate greater than 90%.1Incidence of ATAA is increased among individuals with BAV, which has a worldwide prevalence of 1% to 2%,2and among those with a family history of aortic dissection, familial connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome), or Turner syndrome.3Rarely, ATAAs are caused by syphilis or rheumatologic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or Takayasu disease.3Up to 56% of patients with BAV younger than age 30 years have a dilated ascending aorta (diameter 1.1 times greater than expected based on age, sex, and body surface area).2Patients with BAV have an approximately 9-fold increased relative risk for aortic dissection, although their absolute risk is low (0.68% lifetime).2,3A 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline recommended that first-degree relatives of patients with BAV, aortic root or ascending aorta aneurysms, or aortic dissection undergo aortic screening with a TTE, ECG-gated CT angiography, or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the thoracic aorta and that patients with familial BAV and/or thoracic aortic aneurysms should be referred for genetic testing.3 Ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms are frequently diagnosed incidentally on a thoracic CT imaging study. Approximately 95% of patients with ATAA are asymptomatic at diagnosis, and 5% have nonspecific symptoms such as chest pain, back pain, dysphagia, or dyspnea.4Patients with ATAA should be evaluated for connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and family history of BAV, aortic aneurysm, and sudden death should be elicited. A TTE to evaluate left ventricular function, aortic valve, root, and the proximal ascending aorta, and an ECG-gated aortic CT angiogram with contrast, should be obtained. Thoracic aorta MRA is an alternative to CT and has similar sensitivity (100% vs 98%, respectively) and specificity (98% vs 98%, respectively) for aneurysm detection.5 For patients with ATAA, the 2022 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guideline–recommended goal systolic blood pressure is less than 130/80 mm Hg.6The guideline recommends that patients with BAV who have an ascending aortic diameter 5.5 cm or greater undergo surgery to replace the aortic root and ascending aorta. Other surgical indications include ascending aortic cross-sectional area-height ratio 10 cm2/m or greater or aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater with risk factors for aortic dissection such as family history of aortic dissection, rapid aortic growth rate (>0.3 cm/y), or preconception in women with BAV and an aortic diameter 5.0 cm or greater.6,7Patients with ATAA and BAV who do not meet indications for surgery should undergo annual echocardiography, CT, or MRA to assess for rapid aneurysm expansion (>0.3 cm/y) and progression of BAV.6 Surgical repair includes replacement of aneurysmal tissue with a polyester fiber conduit. For patients with ATAA and severe bicuspid aortic valve stenosis (aortic velocity >4 m/s, mean pressure gradient >40 mm Hg, aortic valve area <1.0 cm2) or aortic regurgitation, aortic valve replacement is typically recommended.6Surgery can often be performed through minimally invasive procedures, such as a hemisternotomy.8The 5-year survival rate after ascending aortic and root replacement is 89.9%.9After ATAA surgery, patients should receive surveillance imaging with CT or MRA within 1 year and, if stable, every 5 years thereafter to monitor for progression of aortic dilation.6 A ECG-gated CT angiogram demonstrated a 5.0-cm ATAA with a cross-sectional/height ratio of 11.7 cm2/m (Figure 2). Based on the patient’s aortic aneurysm size and family history of aortic dissection, she met criteria for surgery.3Ascending aortic replacement was performed minimally invasively, with 4 cm of ascending aorta excised and replaced with a polyester fiber conduit. She did not undergo aortic valve repair or replacement due to her young age and absence of aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation. She was discharged after a 4-day hospitalization. At a clinic visit 1 month later, the patient was asymptomatic and blood pressure was 110/80 mm Hg. Aortic surveillance will be performed with a ECG-gated CT scan 12 months postoperatively, and her first-degree relatives were offered screening for BAV and aortic aneurysm.
